reasoning: MU in late 2023 presents one of those genuinely uncomfortable setups where the chart and the fundamentals are pulling hard in opposite directions. The technical case is bearish and fairly clean: the stock formed a double top near $70, broke below its 50-day EMA, MACD crossed negative two weeks prior, RSI is sitting at 41 and trending down, and OBV is declining — all consistent with distribution. That is not noise; that is momentum selling. On the other side, the fundamental argument is compelling precisely because memory is a deeply cyclical commodity business and the cycle appears to be at or near trough. TrendForce projects DRAM and NAND pricing to bottom in Q4 2023 and recover through 2024. MU trades at a P/B of 1.3x, roughly 30% below its 5-year average of 1.85x, and history shows that buying cyclical semiconductor names at P/B below 1.5x has tended to produce strong 18-to-24-month returns. Management guided for sequential revenue growth, and HBM demand from AI accelerators is a structural tailwind layered on top of the cyclical recovery thesis. The tension here is classic: the market is pricing in near-term pain — and it is correct that near-term pain is probable — while the fundamental case is about a recovery that has not yet shown up in earnings. The 200-day SMA around $62 is the likely near-term test, implying 8-to-10% additional downside. But for someone with a 12-to-24-month horizon, the P/B compression and the cycle setup are historically among the more reliable signals this stock generates. My read is that the technicals are right about the next quarter, and the fundamentals are right about the next two years. The conflict is really a timeframe question, not a disagreement about the underlying business trajectory.

AMD is the classic momentum-versus-valuation dilemma amplified by the AI narrative. The technical picture is strong across every timeframe: price above its 20, 50, and 200-day EMAs with the 50-day acting as dynamic support, MACD above the signal line and in positive territory though showing some histogram deceleration, RSI at 68, and OBV confirming institutional flows into the name. ADX at 35 says the trend is established, not exhausted. Against that, the valuation is stretched: trailing P/E at 45x, forward P/E at 32x, both roughly 40% above the five-year average forward P/E of 23x, and P/S at 8.5x sitting in the 90th percentile historically. FCF yield at 2.2% is below the 10-year Treasury, which is a red flag on an absolute basis. The near-term earnings growth story — MI300 GPU ramp for AI, Genoa/Bergamo data center CPU traction — is what the market is paying for, and the question is whether that execution materializes fast enough to justify the multiple. Historical parallels within AMD itself are instructive: similar momentum-valuation conflicts in late 2020 and mid-2021 allowed another 20-to-30% upside before corrections of 25-to-35% followed. The tension is real but with a directional lean: in the immediate term, 1-to-3 months, sentiment and the AI narrative dominate and the probability of continued upside is around 65%. Over 12-to-18 months, valuation gravity becomes the dominant force unless earnings growth accelerates sharply. AMD is not a value buy here — it is a bet on near-perfect execution of its AI accelerator roadmap.

BABA presents probably the most extreme and persistent technical-fundamental conflict in the large-cap universe at this point. On the fundamental side the numbers look almost absurd in isolation: forward P/E around 8.5x against a historical average near 25x, price-to-FCF of roughly 9x, net cash exceeding $60 billion, a $35 billion buyback authorization, and ROE around 10% despite macro headwinds. These metrics on any other large-cap tech would have value investors falling over themselves. But the technical picture tells a completely different story: multi-year downtrend, price persistently below the 200-week SMA, weekly MACD below zero since 2021, rallies to the $80-$85 zone consistently failing at the declining 50-week EMA, and OBV not making higher highs. The divergence score sits in the 98th percentile of historical observations for large-cap tech. The resolution framework here has to acknowledge something the P/E ratio cannot capture: the market is not pricing BABA as a business, it is pricing it as a geopolitical risk instrument. Regulatory actions since 2020, VIE structure concerns, and the threat of delisting from US exchanges are not quantifiable through standard DCF analysis. Historical precedent from Tencent's 2021-2022 decline shows that technical downtrends in Chinese large-caps can persist 18-to-24 months even when fundamentals are intact. The long-term case — reversion to even 12-15x P/E implies 50-80% upside — requires a fundamental shift in the geopolitical and regulatory environment, not just business execution. That catalyst is binary and unpredictable, which means the technical weakness is a rational market response to an unquantifiable risk premium, not simply market inefficiency.

ADBE is what I would call a fallen angel setup — the business quality is genuinely excellent but the stock has been hammered by two converging forces: macro multiple compression in high-duration growth assets and the existential question mark that generative AI has placed over its creative software moat. The technical damage is real: trading around $460, 28% off the 52-week high, well below both the 50-day EMA at $495 and the 200-day SMA at $540, a death cross formation, RSI at 32 approaching oversold, and high-volume nodes in the $550-$600 range now serving as overhead resistance. On the fundamental side the quality metrics remain genuinely elite: gross margins near 88%, operating margin at 35%, ROE of 31%, ROCE of 25%, forward P/E compressed to roughly 28x from above 40x historically, FCF yield at 4.1%. The PEG ratio of 1.9 is defensible for a business of this durability. The historical precedent within ADBE is encouraging: similar technical-fundamental divergences in 2018 and early 2022 both ultimately resolved in favor of fundamentals, with the stock recovering strongly over 12-to-24 months — but not before an additional 10-to-15% drawdown first. The near-term path is likely a test of the $420-$435 support zone, driven by AI disruption fear (Sora, Midjourney) and macro headwinds. The long-term case rests on whether Firefly can be a genuine AI moat expansion rather than just a defensive response. My read is that the fundamental quality is real and the current discount is excessive, but timing a bottom here is hazardous given the overhang from AI competition narrative.

MU in this scenario presents the mirror image of index 640 — here the technicals are screaming bullish while the fundamentals are flashing caution. The setup: golden cross confirmed two months ago, price at $85.10 making a new 52-week high and trading 12% above the 50-day EMA, RSI at 78.5 entering overbought but sustainable in strong cyclical recoveries, MACD histogram positive and expanding, ADX at 42 signaling a very strong trend, and OBV confirming institutional accumulation with the $70-$74 zone now acting as established support. The fundamental concern is real though: no trailing P/E due to recent losses, forward P/E of 18.5x is 20% above the five-year average of 15.4x, P/S at 4.5x sits in the 90th percentile of the 10-year range, and P/B of 2.1x is a 40% premium to the five-year average. The market is clearly pricing in a cyclical recovery that has not yet materialized in reported numbers. The key insight here is that for a highly cyclical semiconductor name, momentum signals during a post-trough recovery phase are actually more informative leading indicators than trailing valuation metrics. The business is recovering; the P/E looks stretched only because earnings are still depressed. If the DRAM and NAND recovery plays out as projected into 2024-2025, the forward multiples will compress rapidly as earnings accelerate. For a 3-to-6 month horizon, the momentum case has the edge at 65% weight. For a 12-month horizon, the question shifts to whether the recovery trajectory justifies the multiple expansion already priced in. The valuation is not irrational for a cycle recovery — it is stretched relative to history, but the historical averages include trough valuations, which distorts the comparison.
